text.p: Bank of Queensland Ltd, which has rebuffed the Queensland state government's offer to join its state mega-bank merger, said it is considering withdrawing its offer to buy back most of the government's 44 percent stake.

However, the withdrawal of the bank's offer to buy back 30 percent of the government's stake was only temporary and could be revived at a later date, Bank of Queensland chairman Neil Roberts told Reuters in an interview.
"The government has indicated that treasury has it hands full with other issues and while they concentrate on that, it (Treasury) doesn't want to be distracted," Roberts said.
"It's my view that the sensible thing in the short-term is for the Bank of Queensland to withdraw its buy-back proposal."
Roberts stressed that the buy-back offer, first made to the government last May, had not been formally withdrawn yet.
He said the offer, which would cost about A$100 milion at the current market price of the shares, could be revived at a later date, but not in its present form.
"We might make a (buy-back) offer to all shareholders but I'm not addressing this problem at the moment," Roberts said.
He said the Bank of Queensland recognised that the Australian Treasury had given the government three years to sell down their stake.
"They (the government) also have to go back to Federal Treasury and say what progress they have made in selling down that stake," Roberts said.
The Bank of Queensland has distanced itself from the government's merger of Queensland Industry Development Corp, Suncorp Insurance and Finance Group Metway Bank Ltd.
Instead the bank had proposed that the government sell back 30 percent of its holding in Bank of Queensland with the balance of the bank's issued capital, 85 percent held by the public.
"I now think we are shortly to resolve all our problems," Roberts said.

The new mega-bank would hold a three percent stake in Bank of Queensland via an original Metway holding while the government's 44 percent would be quarantined in the government-owned Queensland Treasury Holdings Pty Ltd, Roberts said.

Roberts said the Bank of Queensland board would see three government nominees appointed next month to replace former Suncorp chairman Graham Tucker, fellow director Ted Ranson and Bernard Rowley who announced their retirement this week.
"If we now have a supportive shareholder, that is, the government and three directors who understand they are there to represent all shareholders, all will be well," Roberts said.
"If we can move along that track, the ultimate destination of the (44 percent) shares will be the result of negotiations," he said.
"I don't want to see a repetition of the last six months," Roberts said.
Roberts said the recent events that had led to the formation of Queensland's new banking giant had been a "pressure few months."
"I think we (the bank) are now off the agenda," Roberts said.
"This is a good bank which deserves to be treated as a successful Queensland independent institution," Roberts said.
